question: Will everyone be saved in the end?

answers.label: Yes: in the end evil vanishes and all are restored to God
No: some are lost for ever

overview.text: Origen taught in his own words that God's goodness will recall the whole creation to an end like its beginning, with even his enemies made subject; Augustine reports that he hoped even the devil would be restored. Gregory of Nyssa taught that evil will finally be wiped out, so that God may be "all in all".

His own brother Basil answered that if eternal punishment ends, so does eternal life. Augustine argued the same against the "merciful ones" of his day, and in 543 Justinian anathematized the teaching that punishment is only for a time.

quotes.author: Origen of Alexandria
quotes.english: We hold that the goodness of God, through his Christ, will recall the whole creation to one end, when even his enemies have been made subject to him. ... The end is always like the beginning: as there is one end for all, so there must have been one beginning for all; and as the many have one end, so from one beginning came the many differences and varieties, which are called back again, through the goodness of God and the subjection to Christ and the unity of the Holy Spirit, to one end that is like the beginning.
quotes.original: In unum sane finem putamus quod bonitas Dei per Christum suum universam revocet creaturam, subactis et subiectis etiam inimicis ... Semper enim similis est finis initiis: et ideo sicut unus omnium finis, ita unum omnium intelligi debet initium; et sicut multorum unus finis, ita ab uno initio multae differentiae ac varietates, quae rursum per bonitatem Dei, et subjectionem Christi, atque unitatem Spiritus sancti in unum finem, qui sit initio similis, revocantur
quotes.context: On First Principles survives whole only in Rufinus's Latin translation, which Origen's critics already accused of softening him; the Greek of this chapter is lost apart from fragments. Origen argues from the subjection of Christ's enemies (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25-28) that to be subjected to Christ is to be saved. Quoted from Lommatzsch's 1847 reprint of the Delarue edition, the witness in the store; the library's First Principles book still holds working summaries in place of this text, so the passage still wants a locked library section.

source.edition: Lommatzsch, Origenis Opera Omnia, tomus XXI (Berlin, 1847), De Principiis (Rufinus's Latin)

quotes.author: Origen of Alexandria
quotes.english: So the end, restored to the beginning, and the outcome of things matched with their start, will bring back the state that rational nature had when it had no need to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: every sense of evil will be taken away and wiped perfectly clean, and the one good God alone will become all things to it, not in a few or in many, but in all he himself will be all. When there is nowhere death, nowhere the sting of death, nowhere any evil at all, then truly God will be all in all.
quotes.original: Sic ergo finis ad principium reparatus, et rerum exitus collatus initiis, restituet illum statum, quem tunc habuit natura rationabilis, cum de ligno sciendi bonum et malum comedere non egebat, ut amoto omni malitiae sensu, et ad sincerum purumque deterso, solus qui est unus bonus Deus, hic ei fiat omnia, et non in paucis aliquibus, vel pluribus, sed in omnibus ipse sit omnia. Cum nusquam mors, nusquam aculeus mortis, nusquam omnino malum, tunc vere Deus omnia in omnibus erit.
quotes.context: The closing words of the restoration chapter (numbered section 9 in Lommatzsch's print), again in Rufinus's Latin, glossing 1 Corinthians 15:28: God is all not in some but in all, when evil exists nowhere. Quoted from the same Lommatzsch witness; like 1.6, it still wants a locked library section.

source.edition: Lommatzsch, Origenis Opera Omnia, tomus XXI (Berlin, 1847), De Principiis (Rufinus's Latin)

quotes.author: Origen of Alexandria (as Augustine reports)
quotes.english: Origen believed that even the devil and his angels would be rescued from those torments after severe and long punishment and joined to the holy angels.
quotes.original: misericordior profecto fuit Origenes, qui et ipsum diabolum atque angelos eius post grauiora pro meritis et diuturniora supplicia ex illis cruciatibus eruendos et sociandos sanctis angelis credidit.
quotes.context: Origen's own words survive mainly in Rufinus's softened Latin and in the excerpts his accusers made. Augustine also reports that Origen taught endless cycles of falls and returns.

quotes.author: Gregory of Nyssa
quotes.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
quotes.english: ... meaning that, when evil has at last been wiped out in the long cycles of the ages, nothing will be left outside the good. Even from them there will be one voice confessing the lordship of Christ.
quotes.original: ὅτι τῆς κακίας ποτὲ ταῖς μακραῖς τῶν αἰώνων περιόδοις ἀφανισθείσης, οὐδὲν ἔξω τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καταλειφθήσεται. Ἀλλὰ καὶ παρ' ἐκείνων ὁμοφώνως ἡ ὁμολογία τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ κυριότητος ἔσται.
quotes.context: Gregory's sister Macrina is the teacher in this dialogue. "Them" are those "under the earth" in Philippians 2:10.

quotes.author: Gregory of Nyssa
quotes.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
quotes.english: In this the passage seems to me to teach the complete wiping out of evil. For if God will be in all things that exist, evil will clearly not be among the things that exist. If anyone supposed it still was, how could God be "in all"? Leaving it out would make "all" incomplete.
quotes.original: Ἐν τούτῳ δέ μοι δοκεῖ τὸν παντελῆ τῆς κακίας ἀφανισμὸν δογματίζειν ὁ λόγος. Εἰ γὰρ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς οὖσιν ὁ Θεὸς ἔσται, ἡ κακία δηλαδὴ ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν οὐκ ἔσται. Εἰ γάρ τις ὑπόθοιτο κἀκείνην εἶναι, πῶς σωθήσεται τὸ ἐν πᾶσι τὸν Θεὸν εἶναι; Ἡ γὰρ ὑπεξαίρεσις ἐκείνης, ἐλλιπῆ τῶν πάντων ποιεῖ τὴν περίληψιν.
quotes.context: "God all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28). Gregory was honored as a Father at the council of 381 and later; his hope was not condemned by name.

quotes.author: Basil of Caesarea
quotes.english: ... it is one of the devil's tricks that many people, as if they had forgotten these and so many other sayings and verdicts of the Lord, set an end to punishment for themselves, so as to dare sin all the more. For if eternal punishment will one day have an end, eternal life too will certainly have an end. But if we will not think this of life, what reason is there to set an end to eternal punishment?
quotes.original: ἓν καὶ τοῦτο τῆς μεθοδείας τοῦ διαβόλου, τὸ τοὺς πολλοὺς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὥσπερ ἐπιλαθομέ νους τῶν τοσούτων καὶ τοιούτων τοῦ Κυρίου ῥημάτων καὶ ἀποφάσεων, τέλος κολάσεως εἰς τὸ μᾶλλον κατατολμᾷν τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἑαυτοῖς ὑπο γράφειν. Εἰ γὰρ τῆς αἰωνίου κολάσεως ἔσται ποτὲ τέλος, τέλος ἕξει πάντως καὶ ἡ αἰώνιος ζωή.
quotes.context: The question put to Basil, Gregory of Nyssa's brother: "If one is beaten with many stripes and another with few (Luke 12:47–48), how do some say punishment has no end?" Basil cites Matthew 25:46.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: Now I see I must deal, and peacefully, with our merciful ones, who refuse to believe that the punishment will be everlasting for all, or for some, of those the most just Judge will condemn to hell, but think they will be freed after a fixed time. More merciful still was Origen, who believed that even the devil and his angels would be rescued from those torments after severe and long punishment and joined to the holy angels. But the Church rightly rejected him for this and other things.
quotes.original: Nunc iam cum misericordibus nostris agendum esse uideo et pacifice disputandum, qui uel omnibus illis hominibus, quos iustissimus iudex dignos. gehennae supplicio iudicabit, uel quibusdam eorum nolunt credere poenam sempiternam futuram, sed post certi temporis metas pro cuiusque peccati quantitate longioris siue breuioris eos inde existimant liberandos. Qua in re misericordior profecto fuit Origenes, qui et ipsum diabolum atque angelos eius post grauiora pro meritis et diuturniora supplicia ex illis cruciatibus eruendos et sociandos sanctis angelis credidit. Sed illum et propter hoc et propter alia nonnulla ... non inmerito reprobauit ecclesia
quotes.context: Augustine's "merciful ones" (misericordes) were fellow Catholics. He answers them in the chapters that follow.

quotes.author: Emperor Justinian (Edict against Origen)
quotes.english: If anyone says or thinks that the punishment of demons and of ungodly men is only for a time, and will one day have an end, or that there will be a restoration and return of demons or of ungodly men, let him be anathema.
quotes.original: Si quis dicit aut sentit, ad tempus esse daemonum et impiorum hominum supplicium, eiusque finem aliquando futurum, sive restitutionem et redintegrationem fore daemonum aut impiorum hominum, anathema sit.
quotes.context: Justinian's edict of 543 against Origen, sent to Patriarch Menas of Constantinople: canon 9 of its canons against Origen, as printed in Denzinger's Enchiridion (11th edition, 1911), no. 211. The edition prints the Greek beside the Latin; the scan's Greek is badly garbled by OCR, so the quote follows its clean Latin. Whether the fifteen anathemas of the 553 council repeat this canon is disputed; the 543 edict is the secure text.

gaps.author: Origen of Alexandria
gaps.why: Quoted in Origen's own words (Rufinus's Latin) from the Lommatzsch witness: origen-principiis-1-6 and origen-principiis-3-6. Still open: the library's origen-principiis book holds working summaries, not the text; lock the real De Principiis text (Koetschau, GCS 22, 1913) as library sections.

gaps.author: Isaac of Nineveh
gaps.why: The Syriac voice for final restoration.
gaps.source_hint: Syriac manuscript Bodleian syr. e. 7; Chialà edition (copyright) as note
